items.abstract: Abstract The conscious Turing machine (CTM) is a model of consciousness developed by Lenore and Manuel Blum. Just as the Turing machine is an abstract formal model of computation, the CTM is an abstract formal model of consciousness. It provides a high-level description of processes that might be realised in conscious human beings and other conscious systems. Since it is not a model of brain function, it does not specify how it may be implemented in a living brain. The CTM might even entail false claims about the processes underlying consciousness in human beings. It is thus not obvious how the CTM can explain or contribute to our understanding of consciousness. This paper argues that the CTM may provide different forms of scientific understanding. It may provide a deepened understanding by generalising explanations provided by empirical theories of consciousness. It may also provide mathematical explanations of algorithmic properties. Whether the CTM actually provides these forms of understanding largely depends on whether it constitutes an accurate model of (human) consciousness. This is mostly an empirical question. Other forms of understanding, however, may not dependent on the CTM’s accuracy. Therefore, I also discuss to what extent the CTM may deepen our understanding of consciousness by enabling how-possibly explanations and non-explanatory understanding by unification.
items.title: A Philosophy of Science Perspective on the Conscious Turing Machine

items.abstract: Abstract Philosophers of memory often assume that the extended mind hypothesis is compatible with the causal theory of memory. For extracranial resources can, the idea goes, sustain the causal connection between a past event and a present representation of it that, on causalist views, distinguishes genuine remembering. Some go as far as to claim that constructive versions of the causal theory can accommodate complementarity-based versions of the extended mind hypothesis. This paper casts doubt on these ideas by defending two claims. First, the existing arguments for compatibility are flawed. While some conflate external information storage with cognitive extension, others wrongly hold that fulfilling the conditions for cognitive extension secures the appropriate kind of causal connection for remembering. Second, constructive versions of the causal theory and complementarity-based versions of the extended mind hypothesis are in fact incompatible. For constructive causal theories require of memory traces features that functionally disparate but complementary extracranial resources systematically lack. The paper concludes by considering how parity-based versions of the extended mind hypothesis might fare within the causal theory, and how other theories of memory might be assessed for compatibility with the extended mind hypothesis.
items.title: Mnemic Extension and Appropriate Causation

items.abstract: Permanent, multigenerational human settlement beyond Earth is usually framed as a technological, biomedical and political challenge. This article argues that it is also a problem of procreative ethics. If a settlement depends on local reproduction for long-term continuity, reproduction becomes tied to demographic viability, life-support capacity, genetic diversity, labor needs, and collective survival. Under these conditions, procreative ethics may become a limit on morally permissible settlement: biologically feasible reproduction may require forms of governance incompatible with reproductive autonomy and justice. The article distinguishes three ideal–typical models. Moral exceptionalism permits restrictions on reproductive rights for the sake of survival, risking authoritarian and gendered governance. Moral homogeneity holds that basic reproductive rights and moral principles remain valid across environments, even when their practical application varies with circumstances. A third model, critical procreative ethics informed by antinatalist thought, does not reject procreation but requires heightened justification when prospective lives are created under severe structural and technological constraints. Drawing on feminist bioethics, reproductive justice, environmental limits, space genomics and germline gene editing, the article proposes ethical thresholds for reproduction in future settlements and argues that species survival cannot override reproductive autonomy, justice and the welfare of future persons.
items.title: Procreative ethics as a limit on future space settlement

items.abstract: Abstract Agentic AI systems now act, rather than merely advise, within social and institutional settings. The persistent gap lies less in principles than in deciding which obligations a deployment should attract as the relationships around it change. Risk-based regulation classifies by declared intended purpose and does not register the dependence that forms around a system once it is in use. We propose the Onto-Relational-Sophic (ORS) framework, whose core contribution is to treat that dependence, rated as social embedding, as a trigger for reclassification. A system-in-deployment is rated on autonomy, social embedding, and moral relevance; each rating triggers a module of obligations on providers, deployers, and institutions; nine explicit rules govern assignment, conflicts, and reclassification, including the rating of multi-agent ensembles as wholes and the prospective rating of systems designed to induce dependence; and categories serve as summary labels. Two supporting pillars, grounded in Cyberism, structure the framework: a Cyber-Physical-Social-Thinking ontology that organises the evidence for each rating, and Cybersophy, an axiology that applies a reversibility priority when principles conflict. Three scenarios and a structured comparison with existing EU law show where ORS converges with current obligations and where it adds to them, most clearly when people come to depend on one certified system in different ways. No legal personality is conferred on any system. The rating scales and rules are proposed rather than validated: the social-embedding instrument has not been tested for inter-rater reliability, and the worked classifications rest on the authors’ own ratings. A reliability study should precede regulatory use.
items.title: Governing Agentic AI: An Onto-Relational-Sophic (ORS) Framework for Deployment-Sensitive Governance

items.abstract: This commentary synthesises three strands of documentation compiled on the war in Gaza: (i) findings and proceedings from international judicial, quasi-judicial, and expert bodies; (ii) reporting on the Israeli military’s use of AI-assisted targeting and surveillance systems; and (iii) the record of technology-sector involvement through cloud and AI service contracts. It is important to state at the outset that, with the exception of binding provisional orders from the International Court of Justice and arrest warrants issued by the International Criminal Court, the great majority of the findings discussed below are expert reports, NGO assessments, or investigative journalism—not judicial determinations of individual or state responsibility. They are treated here as documented allegations and assessments, not as adjudicated fact, and where available, the positions of the Government of Israel, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF), and the companies concerned disputing specific characterisations are noted. We situate each strand within the relevant legal framework—the Genocide Convention, international humanitarian law (IHL) on distinction, proportionality, and precaution, and the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights—and we assess the evidentiary weight and the principal uncertainties attached to each. We conclude that the three strands describe a single, interlocking system whose consequences for the civilian population of Gaza are severe, and whose accountability mechanisms remain, as of this writing, largely unresolved.
items.title: Legal findings, algorithmic targeting, and corporate complicity: a commentary on the Gaza conflict’s documentation record

items.abstract: Abstract This article offers an ideology critique of the European Court of Human Rights’ jurisprudence on housing. It argues that the court does not just operate within, but actively sustains, a capitalist understanding of housing. The article thus exposes the role of European human rights law in configuring the relation of politics to the economy in the housing sphere. This is crucial given the fundamental role that housing plays in capitalism as the largest and most significant asset class today. Bringing together insights from ideology critique with the literature on the political economy of housing under capitalism, the article dissects the judicial tools commonly adopted by the court in its case law; the determination of the definitional scope of protection; the margin of appreciation; and proportionality. By tracing the application of these tools across the court’s case law on access to housing, evictions and rent control under Article 8, read in tandem with the case law under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights, the article demonstrates that the court’s judgments undertake an ideological function. In doing so, it shows that the court’s treatment of housing is structured by a capitalist logic whereby the court legitimates the use of housing as a means of profit while it simultaneously refuses to recognise a right of access to housing, abstracts away the social relations of rent to the detriment of tenants and naturalises the protection of private property as common sense.
items.title: Housing Before the European Court of Human Rights: A Critique of Ideology

items.abstract: Abstract Good pharmaceutical innovation policy requires good data about R&D costs. By looking at the economics of the pharmaceutical R&D process, with the use of accurate data about costs, risks, and returns, policymakers can more accurately respond to competing claims for access and incentives to innovate and find ways of promoting affordable, accessible, and innovative drugs while discouraging redundant investments in high cost, low value added drugs. If our pharmaceutical innovation policy goal is truly to make positive contributions to public health, this kind of data should be readily available in usable forms for all drugs and should be used to inform public spending and the design of regulatory incentives.
items.title: Informing Pharmaceutical Innovation Policy: The Health Value of R&D Cost Transparency

items.abstract: Abstract C. D. Broad gives an account of common sense morality on which rightness is a function of fittingness and utility. He claims that this account avoids worries that Sidgwick raises about common sense morality. He also raises a doubt about fittingness that resembles current evolutionary debunking arguments. I present and evaluate Broad’s arguments.
items.title: C. D. Broad on Sidgwick and Common Sense Morality
Privacy and Cybersecurity Guardrails for AI in Healthcare: Consensus-Based Guidance
The Patient-Regarding Reasons Principle: A New Intervention Principle for Surrogate Decisions
Who Should Do Clinical Ethics Work? Defining Appropriate Roles for the “Ethics-Interested”

items.abstract: Abstract This paper argues that Ruth Millikan’s official definitions in Language, Thought, and Other Biological Categories admit persistence-based direct proper functions. These definitions do not require reproductions to involve numerically distinct persisting items, thus supporting a broader account than her surrounding prose suggests. I demonstrate how this interpretation extends through Millikan’s first-order machinery and into her definition of direct proper function. Accordingly, direct proper functions can be conferred on synapses via synapse selection and, more implausibly, on rocks via rockfalls. I examine three strategies for blocking this result: a reproduction requirement, a population requirement, and a service requirement. Given Millikan’s explanatory aims, I argue that she should reject these as general requirements, but accept them for theoretically important subclasses.
items.title: Millikan, Persistence, and Direct Proper Functions: A Slippery Rockslide?
The Case for Models and Modeling in Philosophy of Psychiatry
One Life to Lead: The Mysteries of Time and the Goods of Attachment

items.abstract: Analogy is recognized as a heuristic and rhetorical resource in economics, but economists have paid less attention to its epistemic function and to how to assess competing analogies. Bringing critical realism into dialogue with analogical hermeneutics supports an onto-hermeneutic approach to analogy in which analogical transfer is constrained by the target domain’s causal properties and empirical evidence. An analogy can structure and interpret economic representations without validating them. Here, proportional adequacy provides a criterion for distinguishing legitimate relational transfers. This allows plural economic approaches and representations while preserving empirical accountability and avoiding the treatment of alternative analogies as epistemically equivalent.
items.title: Analogy as Conceptual Infrastructure: Rethinking the Ontology and Methodology of Economics

items.abstract: In Cognitive Science and the Reconceptualization of Social Theory , Stephen P. Turner naturalizes the social sciences, replacing concepts like culture and norms with a deflationary neurobiological approach. This review acknowledges the rigor of his critique against disembodied entities but argues his sociological eliminativism encounters a severe epistemological limit. By reducing human thought to sub-discursive pattern recognition, Turner dismisses the essential explanatory role of symbolically mediated meaning. Dispensing with the semantic nature of understanding renders the genesis of culture, language, and social action incomprehensible. By sacrificing subjectivity, this attempt to ground social theory in neurobiology fails to account for social life.
items.title: The Squirrel, the Symbol, and the Social: On Stephen Turner’s Naturalistic Reconstruction of Social Theory
